latin.152: CAPUT XIV. Nullam extare in manuscriptis libellis rationem quae peccati Adamici imputationem immediatam seu antecedentem probare possit. De Argumentis typis excusis, quae mihi legere contigit, dictum est, ut ego arbitror, satis. Manuscriptorum vidi complura: Sed in quibus nihil fere animadverti, quod non legatur in scriptis Typographorum opera publicatis; si primum illud excipias, cui Placeus manuscripto illo respondit, quod D. Garissolius posterius appellavit, et in quo refellendo magnam partem libri sui consumpsit.
latin.153: Quare nihil mihi videtur consultius, quam ut manuscriptum illud Placei tibi, Lector, exhibeam (Cur enim in illis argumentis vel proponendis, vel refutandis operam meam ponerem, cum id jam fuerit ab ipso Placeo praestitum?) ac, quando id refutare voluit D. Garissolius, ejusque passim frustula et lacinias transcripsit in suum librum, et quantum potuit, confutavit, subjiciam singulis illis particulis viri illius reprehensiones, hisque ipsis Placei defensiones. Ita poteris, Lector aequissime, admodum facile, et citra errandi aleam, de tota hac causa cognoscere, et judicium ferre: id quod alioqui difficile, ne dicam impossibile, foret. Vix enim qua mente, quo sensu quidque dictum fuerit, bene perspici potest, cum lacerae tantum, et suis locis revulsae, ac veluti luxatae et dissipatae partes sermonis legenti offeruntur. Neque est quod quisquam propterea offendatur. Si quid enim in eo scripto reprehensione dignum est, id in iis potissimum partibus habere locum putandum est, quae jam sunt a D. Garissolio vulgatae. Non eo quidem consilio a Placeo compositum fuerat ut ederetur, et ex nimia festinatione irrepsere fortasse nonnulla, si per otium licuisset autori, emendanda atque expolienda: tamen ne voculam quidem tollere, addere, aut mutare voluimus, ne quis de nostra fide vel synceritate conqueri posset. Qualecunque est, Tu aequissime Lector, illud aequi bonique consules, quodque ejus integri legendi, totiusque istius controversiae dijudicandae copiam tibi facimus, aut habebis nobis gratiam, aut saltem non iniquo animo feres.
latin.154: MANUSCRIPTUM POSTERIUS, HOC EST, EXAMEN Tractatus singularis, De peccato originis, in quo demonstratur primum primi hominis peccatum omnibus hominibus imputari, oppositi Thesibus de statu hominis lapsi ante gratiam, disputatis Salmurii die 16. Martii An. 1640. sub Praesidio Josue Placei S. Theologiae Professoris in Academia Salmuriensi. CAPUT I. Capita doctrinae de Peccato originali de quibus inter nos convenit. LICEAT mihi, quaeso, Vir reverende, te, perinde ac si coram sermone res ageretur, compellare et alloqui: Sic enim, uti spero, tua, velut oculis meis obversantis praesentia me torpentem excitabit, et ad tui majorem reverentiam componet. Tu quidem pro tua singulari prudentia voluisti tibi viam ad statum controversiae constituendum munire, praestratis iis de quibus inter nos convenit. Quod tuum consilium valde probo; sed (quod cum tua bona venia dictum velim) visus es mihi neutrum praestitisse satis accurate et enucleate. Patere igitur ut utrumque tuo exemplo faciam breviter quidem, sed ita tamen, ut ab hac nostra amica collatione omnis, si fieri possit, tollatur confusio, omnis ambiguitas.
latin.155: Ego arcte teneo, accurateque defendo quicquid de peccato originali Ecclesia vere Christiana adversus veteres novosque Pelagianos, et Semipelagianos cum definivit olim, tum his postremis seculis suis publicis confessionibus se credere professa est. Id autem universum Daniel Chamierus, vir suo merito magni apud Ecclesias nostras nominis, statum controversiae inter nos et Pighium ac Salmeronem constituens ad tria capita revocavit. Catholici, inquit, (Protestantes intelligit) certis argumentis docent, ipsi humanae naturae inesse corruptionem, seu pravitatem cuilibet homini propriam, aliam ab actibus peccati. Secundo, etiam nascenti homini cuilibet eandem inesse. Tertio eandem ab Adamo ortum ducere, et per propagationem derivari in posteros. Quamvis autem subjungat, haec tria capita continere universam peccati originalis naturam. Itaque iis demonstratis nihil fore reliqui factum; tamen uberioris explicationis causa duo addam: unum, hanc corruptionem omnes animae nostrae facultates ita depravasse, ut nisi ex aqua et Spiritu renati fuerimus, neque ullum fructum vere bonum proferre, neque ad Deum converti valeamus. Alterum, hanc corruptionem vere peccatum esse, omnes Adami posteros, solo Christo, in quo nunquam fuit, excepto, mortis aeternae reos peragens.
latin.156: GARISSOLIUS. Chamierus duo in Peccato originali manifeste distinguit, quod poena est peccati primi, et quod vitium est internum in nobis haerens. Sed prius non veniebat in controversiam cum Pighio, et aliis quos eo libro refutat; itaque eam considerationem non urget hoc loco. Sed quaerebatur tantum, an peccatum originale veram haberet rationem vitii et corruptionis. Affirmat Chamierus, et probat; Et peccatum originale considerans jam, qua vitium est, haud immerito ejus naturam in illis tribus constituit. PLACEUS. Quorsum spectet ista distinctio, nescio? Quis enim unquam peccatum originale dixit esse duplex: unum, poenam peccati primi actualis, alterum, vitium inhaerens; aut duas esse peccati originalis partes: unam poenam peccati primi, alteram peccatum internum in nobis haerens? Sed qui imputationem primi Adae peccati actualis immediatam docent, illi, vel duplex esse dicunt peccatum originale: unum imputatum, alterum inhaerens; vel duas peccati originalis partes; primariam et praecipuam peccatum actuale Adami imputatum, minus praecipuam corruptionem haereditariam. In qua opinione si fuit Chamierus, quomodo in illis tribus, quae commemoravit, universam peccati originalis naturam contineri asseruit? Quomodo addidit; Itaque iis demonstratis nihil erit reliqui factum? Omississet enim praecipuam peccati originalis partem. Adde quod si haeresis Pelagiana in imputationis illius negatione pars sita fuit, ut voluit D. Garissolius, decuit Catholicos eam imputationem inprimis demonstrare, praesertim cum a Stapletono, aliisque nonnullis Pontificiis, aperte negata fuisset. Sed de Chamiero, si opus erit, alibi disputabitur.
latin.157: Tu quidem, observande Symmysta, superiora credis. Sed de hoc ultimo quid sentis? Conceptum est verbis confessionis Ecclesiarum nostrarum Art. XI. quae tu ipse laudas Cap. VII. Credimus hoc vitium esse vere peccatum, quod omnes et singulos homines, ne parvulis quidem exceptis adhuc in utero matrum delitescentibus, aeternae mortis reos coram Deo peragit. Affirmamus quoque hoc vitium, etiam post baptismum, esse vere peccatum, quod ad culpam attinet. Hoc ego ex animo credo ut sacris literis consentaneum, immo rationi, neque everti potest, quin eo ipso thesium mearum quas oppugnas compactio et contextus luxetur. Tu vero num id credis? videris tale quid affirmare Cap. I. et II. tui tractatus, et aliis aliquot locis: sed vereor ne ita loquaris occultandae opinionis tuae gratia: Id enim aliis quibusdam locis exerte negas, eaque negatione tanquam fundamento pars non contemnenda hujus tuae disputationis nititur. Recognosce tua verba: non enim gravabor huc transferre. Cap. V. sic colligis, Ubi mors regnat, nec est reatus ex peccato proprio actuali, ibi necessario est imputatio reatus primi peccati. Item, Cap. V. mors regnavit in infantes. Ergo infantibus reatus primi peccati necessario fuit imputatus. Cum autem videres tibi responderi posse, reatum in illis esse a vitio inhaerente et depravatione haereditaria, tu hanc responsionem cavillum appellasti, et contra sic conclusisti, si pueri in utero matrum, aut recens nati, sunt peccatores, ideo sunt, vel quod actu peccaverint, vel quod primum peccatum primi parentis ipsis imputetur. Tertium siquidem dari non potest, quod illos constituat peccatores. Nam peccator quis dicitur ob peccatum; Nec ullum aliud peccatum potest imputari, nisi illud primum. Relege, si placet, quae sequuntur. Cap. IX. mentem tuam plenius aperis. Non video, inquis, quid sit peccatum originis si negetur ejusmodi imputatio. Potuisset-ne Pighius suam sententiam exprimere clarius?
latin.158: Subjicis rationem: nam quinam mors regnavit tunc in eos quoque qui non peccaverunt ad similitudinem transgressionis Adam, si hoc peccatum Adami non fuit illis imputatum? Finge puerum recens natum vel in utero ipso matris morientem, quid in illo est quod peccatum dici possit? voluntas in ipso ab omni actione vacat, nec potest propria voluntate peccare. Habet in se, inquies, semina peccati, valeat, sed nondum peccatum proprie, nisi peccatum illud originis, quo in Adamo peccavit. Ergo peccatum illius non in ipso, vel ex seipso, sed in prima origine, id est, in primo parente quaerendum est: Nec est aliud peccatum illud quam inobedientia illa voluntaria Adami etc. Tu igitur nullum peccatum originale agnoscis praeter primum illud peccatum actuale Adami nobis imputatum, nullum reatum in infantibus praeter eum qui immediate ex illa imputatione existit. Quo ergo vel animo, vel sensu, corruptionem inhaerentem modo simpliciter peccatum, modo cum epitheto peccatum originale appellas? sic enim in hanc tuam disputationem ambiguitatem et confusionem intulisti, noxiam mihi futuram nisi eam deprehendissem, ac, quod facio, sustulissem. Hic subit animum meum mirari, vir reverende, qui, cum tam aperte a confessione Ecclesiae nostrae abeas, potueris inducere in animum tuum, ut mihi, qui illi religiose adhaereo, quasi ab ea defcivissem, grandem dicam scriberes. Dolet etiam mihi quod te aliis doctrina et sanctitate praelucentem, et quem ex animo diligo, tueri non possim vel ab inconstantia, vel a dissimulatione: ab inconstantia quidem si corruptionem inhaerentem vere peccatum esse, reatum mortis aeternae ex sese fundens modo sensisti, modo non sensisti; a dissimulatione vero, si cum sentires constanter non esse peccatum, tu tamen peccatum esse aliquot locis dixisti et inculcasti, perinde ac si revera et proprie peccatum esse crederes, nec eo contentus, affirmasti inter nos ea de re nullam esse dissensionem, cum te fugere non posset, non solum me, quem refutandum sumpseras, sed Ecclesias etiam nostras vitium illud formaliter et proprie, et, ut loquitur confessio fidei, vere peccatum esse statuere; et eos ipsos, qui tecum imputationem primi peccati urgent, solitos esse peccatum originale in duo peccata dispescere, imputatum et inhaerens, ac suum utrique proprium Mortis aeternae reatum attribuere. Laudarem testimonia nisi libri omnibus noti essent, omnium triti manibus. Hic igitur aut consentis corruptionem haereditariam, seposito peccato Adami imputato, esse vere peccatum damnando generi humano sufficiens, aut dissentis. Si consentis, revoca eas rationes et solutiones, quas in progressu hujus tui tractatus contrariae hypothesi superstuxisti. Si dissentis, haec erit inter me teque unum singularis controversia, quam libentissime suscipiam pro tuenda confessione Ecclesiarum nostrarum, quae mihi videtur verissima.

pass_a.152: CHAPTER XIV. That there exists in manuscript booklets no reason which can prove the immediate or antecedent imputation of Adam's sin. Concerning the arguments printed in type which it has fallen to me to read, it has been said, as I judge, enough. Of manuscripts I have seen many: but in which I have observed almost nothing that is not read in writings published by the work of printers; if you except that first one to which Placeus replied by that manuscript which D. Garissoles called the later one, and in refuting which he consumed a great part of his book.
pass_a.153: Wherefore nothing seems to me more advisable than that I exhibit that manuscript of Placeus to you, Reader (For why would I put my labor either in proposing or in refuting those arguments, when that has already been performed by Placeus himself?) and, when D. Garissoles wished to refute it, and transcribed its scraps and patches passim into his own book, and as far as he could confuted it, I will subjoin to each of those particles that man's censures, and to these very ones Placeus's defenses. So you will be able, most equitable Reader, quite easily, and without the hazard of erring, to know this whole cause and to give judgment: which otherwise would be difficult, not to say impossible. For scarcely can it be well discerned with what mind, in what sense, each thing was said, when only torn parts of the discourse, torn from their places and as it were dislocated and scattered, are offered to the reader. Nor is there reason that anyone should take offense on that account. For if anything in that writing is worthy of censure, it is to be thought to have place especially in those parts which have already been published by D. Garissoles. It had indeed not been composed by Placeus with the design that it should be edited, and from too great haste perhaps some things crept in which, if leisure had been allowed the author, were to be emended and polished: yet we have wished not even to remove, add, or change a little word, lest anyone be able to complain of our faith or sincerity. Whatever it is, you, most equitable Reader, will take it in good part, and because we give you the opportunity of reading it whole and of judging this whole controversy, you will either thank us, or at least bear it with no unfair mind.
pass_a.154: THE LATER MANUSCRIPT, THAT IS, AN EXAMINATION of a singular Tractate, On original sin, in which it is demonstrated that the first sin of the first man is imputed to all men, opposed to Theses on the state of fallen man before grace, disputed at Saumur on the 16th of March in the year 1640 under the presidency of Josue Placeus, Professor of Sacred Theology in the Academy of Saumur. CHAPTER I. Heads of doctrine on Original Sin concerning which we agree among ourselves. Let it be permitted me, I ask, reverend Sir, to address and speak to you just as if the matter were being handled in conversation face to face: for so, as I hope, your presence, as if meeting my eyes, will arouse me who am sluggish, and will compose me to greater reverence toward you. You indeed by your singular prudence wished to fortify for yourself a way to establishing the state of the controversy, having first laid down those things concerning which we agree among ourselves. Which counsel of yours I greatly approve; but (which I would wish said with your good leave) you have seemed to me to have performed neither with enough accuracy and clearness. Suffer therefore that I do both by your example briefly indeed, yet so that from this our friendly conference all confusion, if it can be done, may be removed, all ambiguity.
pass_a.155: I hold tightly, and accurately defend, whatever the truly Christian Church has defined of old against the old and new Pelagians and Semipelagians concerning original sin, and in these last ages has professed by her public confessions that she believes. And that whole Daniel Chamier, a man of great name by his own merit among our Churches, establishing the state of the controversy between us and Pighius and Salmeron, has reduced to three heads. Catholics, he says (he understands Protestants), teach by sure arguments that there is in human nature itself a corruption, or pravity proper to each man, other than the acts of sin. Secondly, that the same is in each man even as he is being born. Third, that the same takes its rise from Adam, and by propagation is derived into posterity. Although he subjoins that these three heads contain the whole nature of original sin—and therefore when they are demonstrated nothing will be left remaining—yet for the sake of fuller explanation I will add two things: one, that this corruption has so depraved all the faculties of our soul that unless we have been born again of water and the Spirit, we can neither bring forth any truly good fruit nor be converted to God. The other, that this corruption is truly sin, making all Adam's posterity, Christ alone excepted, in whom it never was, guilty of eternal death.
pass_a.156: GARISSOLES. Chamier manifestly distinguishes two things in Original Sin: that it is the penalty of the first sin, and that it is an internal vice inhering in us. But the former did not come into controversy with Pighius and others whom he refutes in that book; therefore he does not urge that consideration in this place. But it was asked only whether original sin had the true character of vice and corruption. Chamier affirms and proves; and considering original sin now as it is vice, not without desert he constitutes its nature in those three. PLACEUS. Whither that distinction looks, I know not. For who ever said original sin is twofold: one, the penalty of the first actual sin, the other, inherent vice; or that there are two parts of original sin: one the penalty of the first sin, the other an internal sin inhering in us? But those who teach the immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin say either that original sin is twofold—one imputed, the other inherent—or that there are two parts of original sin; the primary and chief the imputed actual sin of Adam, the less chief hereditary corruption. If Chamier was of that opinion, how did he assert that in those three which he recounted the whole nature of original sin is contained? How did he add, Therefore when these are demonstrated nothing will be left remaining? For he would have omitted the chief part of original sin. Add that if the Pelagian heresy was partly situated in the denial of that imputation, as D. Garissoles wished, it behooved Catholics to demonstrate that imputation first of all, especially since it had been openly denied by Stapleton and some other Papists. But of Chamier, if there will be need, it will be disputed elsewhere.
pass_a.157: You indeed, observant fellow-initiate, believe the foregoing. But of this last what do you feel? It is framed in the words of the confession of our Churches, Article XI, which you yourself praise in Cap. VII: We believe this vice to be truly sin, which makes all and singular men, not even little ones excepted still hiding in the womb of mothers, guilty of eternal death before God. We also affirm that this vice, even after baptism, is truly sin as far as guilt is concerned. This I believe from the heart as agreeing with the sacred letters, nay with reason, and it cannot be overturned without the very compacting and context of my theses which you attack being disordered. But do you believe it? You seem to affirm such a thing in Cap. I and II of your tractate and in some other places: but I fear you so speak for the sake of hiding your opinion: for in certain other places you expressly deny it, and on that negation as a foundation a not contemptible part of this your disputation rests. Recognize your words: for I will not mind transferring them hither. Cap. V you gather thus: Where death reigns, and there is no guilt from one's own actual sin, there necessarily is imputation of the guilt of the first sin. Likewise Cap. V: death reigned unto infants. Therefore the guilt of the first sin was necessarily imputed to infants. But when you saw it could be answered to you that the guilt in them is from inherent vice and hereditary depravation, you called this reply a cavil, and against it concluded thus: if children in the mothers' womb, or newly born, are sinners, they are so either because they have sinned in act, or because the first sin of the first parent is imputed to them. For a third cannot be given that constitutes them sinners. For one is called a sinner on account of sin; nor can any other sin be imputed except that first. Reread, if you please, what follows. Cap. IX you open your mind more fully. I do not see, you say, what original sin is if such imputation is denied. Could Pighius have expressed his opinion more clearly?
pass_a.158: You subjoin the reason: for how did death then reign even unto those also who did not sin after the likeness of Adam's transgression, if this sin of Adam was not imputed to them? Fancy a child newly born or dying in the very womb of the mother: what is in him that can be called sin? will in him is void of all action, nor can he sin by his own will. He has in himself, you will say, seeds of sin—granted—but not yet sin properly, unless that sin of origin by which he sinned in Adam. Therefore his sin is to be sought not in him, or from himself, but in the first origin, that is, in the first parent: nor is that sin other than that voluntary disobedience of Adam, etc. You therefore acknowledge no original sin besides that first actual sin of Adam imputed to us, no guilt in infants besides that which exists immediately from that imputation. With what mind, then, or sense, do you call inherent corruption now simply sin, now with the epithet original sin? for so you have brought ambiguity and confusion into this your disputation, which would have been harmful to me unless I had detected it and, as I do, removed it. Here it comes upon my mind to wonder, reverend Sir, that you, when you so openly depart from the confession of our Church, could bring it into your mind to write me a great charge as if I, who religiously cling to it, had defected from it. It also grieves me that I cannot defend you, who shine before others in doctrine and holiness, and whom I love from the heart, either from inconstancy or from dissimulation: from inconstancy indeed if you have sometimes felt, sometimes not felt, that inherent corruption is truly sin, pouring forth from itself the guilt of eternal death; from dissimulation truly, if when you constantly felt it is not sin, you nevertheless in some places said and inculcated that it is sin, just as if you truly and properly believed it to be sin, and not content with that, affirmed there is no dissent between us on that matter, when it could not escape you that not only I, whom you had taken to refute, but also our Churches establish that vice formally and properly, and, as the confession of faith speaks, to be truly sin; and that those very ones who with you urge the imputation of the first sin are accustomed to divide original sin into two sins, imputed and inherent, and to attribute to each its own proper guilt of eternal death. I would praise testimonies unless the books were known to all, worn by the hands of all. Here therefore you either consent that hereditary corruption, the imputed sin of Adam being set aside, is truly sin sufficient for damning the human race, or you dissent. If you consent, revoke those reasons and solutions which in the progress of this your tractate you have built upon the contrary hypothesis. If you dissent, this will be between me and you one singular controversy, which I will most gladly undertake for defending the confession of our Churches, which seems to me most true.

152: Chapter XIV. That no argument in the manuscript pamphlets can prove the immediate or antecedent imputation of Adam's sin. Of the printed arguments I have managed to read, enough has been said, I judge. I have seen many manuscripts, and in them I have noticed almost nothing that is not already in books issued by the printers—save that first piece to which Placeus answered in the manuscript Garissoles later called the later one, and on whose refutation Garissoles spent a great part of his book.
153: Nothing therefore seems wiser than to set that Placeus manuscript before you, Reader (why should I spend myself proposing or answering those arguments when Placeus has already done it?), and, since Garissoles chose to refute it and copied its scraps and patches into his own book and answered them as he could, to set under each scrap that man's censures and Placeus's own defenses. So you, most fair Reader, may know the whole cause easily and without risk of error, and judge—which would otherwise be hard, not to say impossible. One can scarcely see with what mind or sense each thing was said when only torn, uprooted, and scattered pieces of the discourse are offered. Let no one take offense at that. If anything in the writing deserves blame, it is chiefly in the parts Garissoles has already published. Placeus did not compose it to be printed, and haste may have left spots he would have polished at leisure; yet we would not drop, add, or change even a word, lest anyone doubt our honesty. Take it, most fair Reader, in good part: we give you the whole to read and the whole controversy to judge—thank us, or at least bear it without ill will.
154: THE LATER MANUSCRIPT, that is, an Examination of a singular tractate On original sin, which argues that the first man's first sin is imputed to all, set against Theses on the state of fallen man before grace, disputed at Saumur on 16 March 1640 under Josue de la Place, professor of theology there. Chapter I. Heads of doctrine on original sin on which we agree. Let me address you, reverend Sir, as if we spoke face to face: so your presence before my eyes may wake my dullness and tune me to deeper reverence. By your singular prudence you wished to clear the state of the question by first laying down what we hold in common. I much approve that plan; yet (with your leave) you seem to me to have done neither part with enough care and clearness. Allow me therefore to do both after your example—briefly, yet so that from this friendly conference every confusion and ambiguity may, if possible, be cleared away.
155: I hold fast, and carefully defend, whatever the truly Christian Church has defined against old and new Pelagians and Semipelagians on original sin, and what she has professed in these later ages by her public confessions. Daniel Chamier—a man of deserved name among our churches—reduced the whole dispute between us and Pighius and Salmeron to three heads. Catholics (he means Protestants), he says, prove by sure arguments that human nature itself has a corruption or pravity proper to each person, distinct from sinful acts; second, that the same is in each even at birth; third, that it rises from Adam and passes to posterity by propagation. Though he adds that these three contain the whole nature of original sin—so that once proved nothing remains—I still add two points for clearer teaching: first, that this corruption so spoils every faculty of the soul that, unless we are born again of water and the Spirit, we can neither bear any truly good fruit nor turn to God; second, that this corruption is truly sin, and makes all Adam's posterity—Christ alone excepted, in whom it never was—guilty of eternal death.
156: GARISSOLES. Chamier clearly divides two things in original sin: that it is the penalty of the first sin, and that it is an inward vice inhering in us. The first was not in dispute with Pighius and the others he answers in that book, so he does not press it here. The only question was whether original sin has the true character of vice and corruption. Chamier affirms and proves it; and taking original sin as vice, he rightly sets its nature in those three heads. PLACEUS. I do not see what that distinction is for. Who ever called original sin twofold—one the penalty of the first actual sin, the other inherent vice—or made two parts of it, penalty and inward sin? Those who teach immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin do say either that original sin is twofold (imputed and inherent) or that it has two parts—the chief being Adam's imputed actual sin, the lesser hereditary corruption. If Chamier held that, how could he say those three heads contain the whole nature of original sin, or add that once they are proved nothing remains? He would have left out the chief part. And if Pelagian heresy partly lay in denying that imputation, as Garissoles claims, Catholics ought to have proved the imputation first of all, especially since Stapleton and some other Papists openly denied it. Of Chamier, if need be, elsewhere.
157: You, observant colleague, hold the points above. But what of this last? It is cast in the words of our Churches' Confession, Article XI, which you yourself praise in chapter VII: We believe this vice is truly sin, which makes every person—even little ones still hidden in the womb—guilty of eternal death before God. We also affirm that after baptism this vice is still truly sin as to guilt. I believe this from the heart as agreeing with Scripture and with reason; overturn it and the very fabric of the theses you attack comes apart. Do you believe it? In chapters I-II of your tract and elsewhere you seem to say so; yet I fear you speak so to hide your view, for in other places you openly deny it, and a large part of your case rests on that denial. Hear your own words. Chapter V: Where death reigns and there is no guilt from one's own actual sin, there must be imputation of the first sin's guilt. Likewise: death reigned over infants; therefore the first sin's guilt was necessarily imputed to them. When you saw the reply that their guilt comes from inherent vice and hereditary depravity, you called it a cavil and concluded: if children in the womb or newly born are sinners, it is either because they have sinned in act or because the first parent's first sin is imputed to them—for no third way can make them sinners. One is called a sinner because of sin; no other sin can be imputed but that first. Read on. In chapter IX you speak more plainly: I do not see what original sin is if such imputation is denied. Could Pighius have put his mind more clearly?
158: You add the reason: how then did death reign even over those who did not sin after the likeness of Adam's trespass, if Adam's sin was not imputed to them? Picture a newborn, or a child dying in the womb: what in him can be called sin? His will is idle of every act and cannot sin by its own choice. He has, you will say, seeds of sin—granted—but not yet sin properly, except that origin-sin by which he sinned in Adam. So his sin is sought not in him or from himself but in the first origin, the first parent; and that sin is nothing but Adam's voluntary disobedience, and so on. You therefore own no original sin but Adam's first actual sin imputed to us, and no guilt in infants but what springs immediately from that imputation. With what mind, then, do you call inherent corruption now simply sin, now original sin? So you have poured ambiguity and confusion into your case—harmful to me had I not spotted it and, as I do, cleared it away. I wonder, reverend Sir, that you, so openly leaving our Church's confession, could charge me—who cling to it—as if I had deserted it. It also grieves me that I cannot shield you, whom I love and who outshine others in doctrine and holiness, from inconstancy or from dissimulation: inconstancy, if you have sometimes held and sometimes not held that inherent corruption is truly sin and itself yields eternal death's guilt; dissimulation, if while you steadily held it is not sin you still said and pressed in places that it is, as if you truly believed it, and even claimed we do not disagree—when you could not miss that not only I, whom you set out to refute, but our Churches too hold that vice formally and properly, and, as the confession says, truly sin; and that those who with you urge first-sin imputation usually split original sin into two—imputed and inherent—and give each its own guilt of eternal death. I would cite witnesses if the books were not known to all and worn by every hand. So either you grant that hereditary corruption, apart from Adam's imputed sin, is truly sin enough to damn the human race, or you deny it. If you grant it, take back the reasons and answers you built in this tract on the contrary premise. If you deny it, this will be our one special quarrel, which I will gladly take up to defend our Churches' confession, which seems to me most true.
